**On Lichen, and Other Slow Partnerships**

There is a rock behind a house I know, a granite boulder the size of a kneeling cow, and on its north face grows a patch of pale green-gray crust roughly the size of a dinner plate. Nobody planted it. Nobody waters it. It was there when the house was built and it will be there, in some form, when the house is gone. If you visited it every year for the rest of your life with a ruler, you might, with luck and good eyesight, record that it had spread by the width of a fingernail. It is a lichen, and I find I can think about it for a very long time.

I want to write about lichen partly because it is the kind of thing almost nobody thinks about, and partly because once you do start thinking about it, it turns out to be a doorway into nearly everything else: time, cooperation, the failure of categories, the difficulty of seeing what is right in front of you. It also has one of the best origin stories in biology, a story about a man who was right and was punished for it, which is the sort of story that never gets old.

---

Start with what lichen is, because for most of human history nobody knew. Lichens were classified, when they were classified at all, as a kind of moss, or a kind of primitive plant, or a sort of excrescence of the rock itself. The Greek word *leichen* seems to have meant something like "what eats around itself," which is at least observant: lichens do spread outward slowly in rings and crusts, as if consuming the surface they sit on. Linnaeus lumped them in with the algae and the fungi in his vast category of "rustici pauperrimi," the poor peasants of the vegetable kingdom. He did not think highly of them. Almost nobody did.

Then in the late 1860s a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener looked at lichens under a microscope, carefully, and announced something that sounded absurd. A lichen, he said, was not one organism. It was two. There was a fungus, and inside the fungus's woven tissues, held like grain in a granary, were algal cells. The fungus, he thought, was essentially farming the algae—capturing them, enclosing them, and living off the sugars they produced by photosynthesis. He used the language of masters and slaves, which was the language of his century, and it made the idea sound sinister. But the structural claim was the important one: this thing that looks like a single creature is a composite.

The lichenologists of Europe were, to put it gently, not persuaded. They had spent careers cataloguing lichens as species, naming them, arranging them in families. They were not prepared to hear that their subject was a kind of biological contraption. One prominent lichenologist called the theory "sensational romance." Another wrote that the idea of "the unnatural union between a captive algal damsel and a tyrant fungal master" was an insult to common sense. For a couple of decades Schwendener's dual hypothesis was the position of a stubborn minority, argued over in journals, resisted in lecture halls. Beatrix Potter, before she was the author of *Peter Rabbit*, spent years drawing fungi and lichens under the microscope and was one of the amateurs who entered this fray, though the Linnean Society would not let her read her own paper because she was a woman.

Schwendener was right, of course. The evidence accumulated, the resistance died off with the people who had mounted it, and by the early twentieth century it was simply taught as fact that lichens are a symbiosis between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, either a green alga or a cyanobacterium or sometimes both. The word *symbiosis* itself—"living together"—was coined in 1879 by Anton de Bary, and it was lichens he had partly in mind when he coined it. That is worth pausing on. One of the central concepts in modern biology, the one that would eventually explain where mitochondria came from and how coral reefs survive and what your gut is doing right now, was invented to describe the gray crust on a rock.

---

And then the story did something wonderful: it happened again.

In 2016, a researcher named Toby Spribille was trying to understand why two lichens in the mountains of Montana, which had exactly the same fungus and exactly the same alga, looked different. One was yellow and one was brown. They produced different acids. By the textbook they should have been the same organism, and they clearly were not. When he sequenced everything in the lichen tissue rather than just the two partners he expected, he found a third: a basidiomycete yeast, a single-celled fungus from a completely different lineage than the main fungal partner, living in the outer cortex of the lichen. It was in the yellow one in abundance and nearly absent in the brown one. When his team looked further, they found these yeasts in lichens across six continents. They had been there the whole time, in specimens that had been studied for a hundred and fifty years, and no one had seen them.

I love this for the obvious reason, which is that it is humbling. But I love it more for what it says about how seeing works. Nobody found the yeast because nobody was looking for a yeast. The dual hypothesis had won so decisively that it had become a lens, and the lens showed two things, so two things were seen. It took a discrepancy that refused to go away—two identical things that were not identical—to force a different kind of looking. This is, I think, the ordinary texture of knowledge: not steady accumulation but long periods of confident partial sight, punctuated by the discovery that the thing has been more than you thought all along.

There is a line of thinking, associated with Lynn Margulis and with more recent work on the microbiome, that says this is not a quirk of lichens but a general truth about life. Individuals, on this view, are a kind of convenient fiction. What we call an organism is a negotiated settlement among many lineages, some of which have been together so long that they have forgotten they were ever apart. The mitochondria in every one of your cells were once free-living bacteria. The plastids in every leaf were once cyanobacteria, close cousins of the ones that live in some lichens today. Lichens are simply a case where the merger is recent enough, loose enough, that you can still see the seams.

---

What lichens do with their partnership is live in places nothing else can.

They grow on bare rock, on tree bark, on the tops of mountains and the edges of Antarctica, on gravestones and the roofs of cars parked too long. They are estimated to cover something like seven percent of the earth's land surface, which is more than tropical rainforest. They do this by a combination of frugality and patience that is almost unbearable to contemplate. The alga makes sugar from light. The fungus provides structure and water retention and mineral scavenging and, crucially, a kind of enclosure that lets the alga survive drying out completely. When a lichen dries, it simply stops. Its metabolism drops to near zero. It can sit like that for months. When rain comes, it rehydrates within minutes and resumes photosynthesis as if nothing had happened. Some lichens have been revived after years of storage in herbarium cabinets.

This is a different relationship to time than the one most living things have. A mammal that stops eating dies in weeks. A tree that loses its leaves in a drought has a season, maybe two. A lichen simply waits. And because it spends so much of its life waiting, it grows with a slowness that is hard to hold in the mind. Crustose lichens—the flat, painted-on kind—may add a fraction of a millimeter to their radius in a year. Some of the yellow-green map lichens in the Arctic, which grow in a mosaic of tiny tiles that really does look like a map, are thought by some to be thousands of years old. There are patches of lichen that were young when the pyramids were being built.

Glaciologists use this. Because certain lichens grow at a fairly steady rate on fresh rock, you can date how long a boulder has been exposed by measuring the largest lichen on it. This technique, lichenometry, has been used to reconstruct the retreat of glaciers over the last several centuries, to date rockfalls and moraines. The lichen keeps time, not for itself, but incidentally, the way rings in a tree do. It lays down a record simply by living slowly enough to become a clock.

---

And here is a thing about lichens that has always struck me as quietly tragic: they are so good at absorbing what falls on them from the air that they are killed by it.

Lichens have no roots. They take up water and dissolved minerals directly from rain and fog and dew across their whole surface, which means they also take up everything else the atmosphere carries. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, as coal smoke filled the cities of Europe and America, lichens vanished from the urban centers outward. Sulfur dioxide, even in small quantities, destroys the algal partner. Botanists began to speak of "lichen deserts"—zones around industrial towns where nothing grew on the trees or stones, and then gradient zones farther out where only the hardiest species survived, and then, at some distance, the full community returning. You could map air quality by walking outward from a factory and noting which lichens reappeared. They were pollution indicators before anyone thought to design pollution indicators.

The same trait had another consequence. After the Chernobyl reactor exploded in 1986, radioactive cesium drifted across Scandinavia and settled on the tundra. Lichens absorbed it, as they absorb everything. Reindeer eat lichen—vast quantities of it through the winter, when nothing else is available. Within months the reindeer of Sami herders in Norway and Sweden carried levels of cesium-137 far above what was considered safe for human consumption. Tens of thousands of animals were slaughtered and their meat discarded. A way of life that had operated in one of the least industrialized landscapes in Europe was disrupted by a machine a thousand miles away, and the messenger was the humblest organism in the food chain.

There is a kind of moral in this that I resist stating too neatly. But the shape of it is clear enough: the thing that makes lichen so resilient—its openness, its absorption, its willingness to take in whatever comes—is the same thing that makes it a perfect register of harm. It has no way to refuse. It simply records.

---

People have found uses for lichens for as long as there have been people, which is another way of saying that things we fail to notice are not necessarily things we fail to use. The purple dye orchil, extracted from *Roccella* species and used since antiquity, was a cheaper substitute for the murex purple of emperors. Litmus—the acid-base indicator every schoolchild has dipped into vinegar—is a lichen extract. The soft, earthy browns and rusts of traditional Harris Tweed came from "crottle," a lichen scraped off Hebridean rocks and boiled with the wool. In parts of Scandinavia and North America, lichens were famine food, boiled repeatedly to leach out the bitter acids. *Usnea*, the gray-green beard that hangs from conifer branches, was used as a wound dressing; it contains usnic acid, which is genuinely antibacterial. Some perfumes still depend on oakmoss, a lichen, for the low, mossy, forest-floor note in their base.

None of this is why I find lichen worth writing about. I mention it because I think there's a temptation, when praising something small and slow, to make its value entirely aesthetic or philosophical, as if the case for attention rested on lichen being pretty or profound. It is both of those things. But it is also litmus and tweed and antibiotics and reindeer, and I want to hold onto the plain fact that the world is dense with things that matter in ways we have not bothered to trace.

---

In 2005, and again in later experiments, the European Space Agency sent lichens into orbit. Samples of *Rhizocarpon geographicum* and *Xanthoria elegans* were mounted on the outside of a spacecraft and exposed, unshielded, to the vacuum of space, to unfiltered ultraviolet radiation, to temperature swings from far below freezing to well above boiling, for two weeks and later for a year and a half. Then they were brought back and given water. They recovered. They photosynthesized. A crust scraped from a rock in the Alps survived conditions that would kill nearly any other complex organism in minutes.

I don't think this means anything cosmic about lichens. It means that a strategy of radical patience and radical simplicity—stop everything, wait, resume—is more robust than the strategies most of us have adopted. It means that the partnership Schwendener saw, and the deeper partnership Spribille saw beneath it, produces something more durable than any of its parts could have been alone. The alga cannot survive on bare rock. The fungus cannot make sugar from light. The yeast, presumably, cannot do much of anything on its own. Together they outlasted the Roman Empire and a trip to space.

---

I return, in the end, to the rock behind the house and the plate-sized patch on its north face. I do not know how old it is. I do not know how many partners are living inside it, or what fraction of the year it spends in suspended animation, waiting for rain. I do know that every generation of people who have lived in that house have walked past it without a second thought, and that it has taken up, patiently, whatever the wind delivered—soot, pollen, the salt of the sea a few miles off—and kept a record no one has read.

What I take from lichen is not a lesson exactly, because lichen does not teach. It just persists in a way that reframes what persistence can look like. We tend to imagine survival as a matter of strength, or speed, or cleverness. Lichen survives by being several things at once, by holding still, by being porous to the world even when that porousness costs it. It was there before we had a category for it, and it went on being what it was through every century of our misunderstanding, and it will be there, some form of it, after we have stopped looking.

There is more to say. There is always more to say about anything, if you keep looking, which may be the only real point. But the patch on the rock is not in a hurry, and I find, for once, that I am not either.
